philosophyChapters.title: Phenomenology and Existentialism
philosophyChapters.summary: Phenomenalism tries to understand experience in the form it appears in consciousness. Existentialism sharpens within this experience questions of freedom, choice, death, anxiety, futility, responsibility, and authentic life. The two traditions are not to be confused, but there is a deep dialogue between them in many twentieth-century thinkers. Husserl 's famous exhortation to return to the facts does not mean accepting ordinary experience without examination; rather, it means putting theoretical presuppositions into brackets and describing how experience manifests itself. Consciousness is always oriented towards something, this quality is called intentionality. Observe, remember, hope, and fear as the consciousness is oriented towards an object, event, or possibility. Scientific abstraction is important, but human experience is not the only scientific measure. I live first in the world, I walk the streets, I make connections, I use objects, I speak the language, then I describe the scientific. The idea of a world of life shows the importance of this prescient experience. Parallel philosophy sees here the philosophical significance of folk wisdom, language, and everyday experience without scientific criterion. It is insufficient to understand human existence from a different brain-body. I am already inside the world, the tools and relationships, the history and possibilities. Mortality and timeliness change the meaning of a person 's existence. But while acknowledging the philosophical importance of Heidegger, critical discussion of his political history cannot be suppressed. Ethical review is necessary even if the idea and life history are separate questions. Sartre 's famous idea that humans first come into existence and then make meaning out of their choices is read as a declaration of independence against predestined anthropocentrism. The excuse may be an attempt to escape one 's freedom through selfishness and immorality. But parallel philosophies question the freedom of speech. Hunger, caste, patriarchy, poverty, war, disability, imprisonment and state violence limit real possibilities. Later developments of the phenomenological tradition, particularly Merlo-Ponty, regard the body as a medium for experiencing the world and not just objects. I am not just a body. I am a physical being. Sickness, disability, gender, labour and place change the structure of experience. Body experience is important to the dignity-based ethics of Parallel Philosophy. Other people are not just objects of my experience. Its vision is one of desire and freedom. Love, conflict, shame, belief, and violence are all created by the presence of other self-consciousnesses. The question of social justice finds empirical depth here: humiliation is not merely a lack of resources; it is connected to how one is seen and perceived in the public world. A criticism of existentialism has been that it is sometimes overly personal. Parallel philosophy improves on this premise. The advice to choose is hollow when the person 's real options are closed. Freedom does not merely require the lifting of legal restrictions; it also requires education, food, health and safety, social respect, and a minimum level of political voice. Regional languages, migration, floods, agriculture, women 's domestic labour, caste practices, festivals, and folkloric memories make up the world of these experiences. To place this experience in philosophy is not to romanticize public life; it is to structure and describe pain, meaning, and the relationship of being. According to the basic axiom of phenomenology, consciousness is not an empty vessel; it is always oriented towards something, whether seen or remembered, feared or imagined. Objects are not found complete in consciousness at once; their meaning is formed by perception, memory, and possible further experience. Intellectualism is not necessarily a denial of the existence of external things. The question is first how the object manifests itself in experience. Parallel realism describes the structure of experience while holding that objects resist our expectations and allow for cross-examination.

philosophyChapters.title: Analytic Philosophy
philosophyChapters.summary: Analytical philosophy is not a single theory but a broad name for a number of schools of thought in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries that emphasize language, logic, knowledge, science, and the microscopic analysis of mind and concepts. Frege, Russell, Moore, Wittgenstein and many later thinkers developed different directions in this tradition. This is of particular importance for parallel philosophies because the linguistic rigor of the neo-Jurisprudence makes problem-level communication possible, but it is inappropriate to declare a historical equivalence. Frege developed the distinction between statement structure and function, quantifier, and semantic context in modern logic. Russell showed by the analysis of descriptions that grammatical forms and logical forms can be different. Sentences like the one about the current king of France being bald show that ordinary grammar sometimes has hidden claims to existence. Many philosophical fallacies can be traced back to misreadings of linguistic forms. The Tractatus attempts to understand the relationship between language and the world through imagery. Meaningful statements indicate a possible state of the fact. Logic explains the structure of language and the world. But morality, beauty, and the meaning of life can be areas that are not expressed in the same way as factual statements. The impact of this border dispute was profound. In Philosophical Investigations, the point of view changes. The meaning of the word is in their use many times. Language is not a single rigid structure. it is a plurality of languages. Orders, questions, prayers, jokes, calculations, poems, and legal pronouncements are different from the rules of the day. The work of philosophy can sometimes be more about unraveling linguistic riddles than it is about theorizing. The analytic method asks: What is the necessary and sufficient condition of a word like freedom because freedom is a person 's true duty? Although later philosophies showed the limits of strict definition, the value of explicit distinction remained. Parallel philosophy adopts this discipline: social debates based on vague terms quickly become confusing. Analytical philosophy is not just a language game. Much of modern ethics, political philosophy, philosophy of mind, science philosophy, and epistemology developed within this tradition. Analytical clarity is important in Rawls 's theories of justice, contemporary free will, psychoanalytic relationships, personal identity, and artificial intelligence. The neologism develops highly nuanced technical language to describe the relationship, breakdown, lack of knowledge, scope, and linguistic structure. Analytic philosophy also subtracts logical forms, contexts, properties, relations, and conditions of knowledge. With these similarities, a comparative dialogue is possible. But it would be a historical mistake to say that Genghis was Frege or that neo-Nazi was modern symbolic logic. The purpose of the question is different from semiotics and philosophical background. Technical clarity is useful, but if the language becomes too specialized to be penetrated by the wider intellectual community, philosophy may withdraw from social life. Both neoliberalism and modern analytic philosophy are familiar with this criticism. Parallel philosophy proposes a double authorship, requiring subtlety at the technical level and clear explanations for common text. Some philosophical problems may be linguistic fallacies; with correct analysis, the problems disappear. However, not all problems are like that. Poverty, caste discrimination, religious violence, and the climate crisis are not mere words. Analytical clarity explains the problem, and social action is necessary. If ambiguity is the source of confusion, then the work of philosophy must remain only clear definitions and valid arguments. A branch of analytic philosophy looks for the logical form behind simple sentences. Grammatical surfaces sometimes give rise to confusion about existence or relation. The second stream considers ordinary language use, context, and linguistic behavior as the basis of philosophical clarity.

philosophyChapters.title: Pragmatism
philosophyChapters.summary: The fundamental strength of pragmatism is that it does not allow philosophy to become a mere abstract definitional game, cut off from life. In this tradition associated with Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, the relationship between thought, meaning, truth, exploration, experience, and action is repeatedly brought up. But to call pragmatism the truth that it is useful would be to trivialize its serious philosophical nature. Practical results and long-term testing are important for efficacy, but immediate benefit is not a substitute for truth. The basic idea of Peirce 's pragmatic formula is to look for the meaning of a concept in practical differences that that concept produces in possible experiences or actions. If two theories yield the same result under all possible conditions, then their alleged difference may possibly be only semantic. The importance of this method is in reducing philosophical ambiguity. Freedom is a true belief because words like rights are not defined by mere declarations of ideals. One has to ask what difference does this concept make in practice. William James emphasizes the lived and experienced aspects of truth, but caution is required here. A lie can be useful in the short term. Rumors can provide political gain, false medical claims can create markets, and superstitions can provide psychological relief. For this reason, the meaning of the text should be clear to the reader: in what time period, on what evidence, and at what cost. Peirce 's ideas of long-term exploration defend pragmatism from arbitrary individualism. The truth is not only useful to us; it requires a process of public scrutiny, criticism, review, and community inquiry. Parallel philosophy sees from this point onward a confirmation of its error-prone epistemology. Dewey links ideas from problem-solving to education to democracy and social experimentation. Democracy is not just a voting system but can also be a life form of shared exploration, communication and experience-refining. In this view, the question of whether institutions are sacrosanct, whether they solve social problems, whether they enhance civic dignity, and whether they learn from new experiences is essential. If a policy is said to be just in theory but in practice consistently offends or marginalizes certain groups, the policy is worth re-examining. Consequences are an important part of a moral argument. But results are not the only criterion. If the basic rights of the minority are destroyed for the benefit of the majority, then totalitarianism is not an adequate answer. Parallel philosophy therefore examines outcomes, rights and dignity, processes and long-term social impacts simultaneously. In the Nyaya tradition, there is a discussion of right knowledge being associated with successful tendencies; Mīmāṃsā is about karma and karma, and Pāla; Buddhist traditions emphasize the practical aspects of suffering prevention; and many Indian philosophies emphasize the lifelong goal of liberation. However, these similarities should not be declared as direct historical parallels. Parallel philosophies communicate problem-solving and how the relationship between science and life is considered in both traditions. Peirce emphasizes genuine skepticism rather than artificial consensus. Beliefs form habits of action.Investigation begins when experience or opposing factors destabilize these habits. We are only skeptical if we say that not changing one 's behavior or decisions can be philosophical posturing. Persistence, authority, instinct, and the method of public inquiry have a different credibility. The merit of public inquiry is not that the researcher is an impartial deity; rather, the method allows for the correction of personal bias in the long run. The results are not final and are researched by the community. The meaning of a concept is clear when one thinks about what its practical consequences might be. The object is rigid, meaning it opens up under possible pressure and pressure. The meaning of this sutra is truth, not mere immediate gain; the result is the test of perception.

philosophyChapters.title: Philosophy of Science
philosophyChapters.summary: Science is not just a list of facts. Science is a complex process of questioning, hypothesizing, observing, measuring, experimenting, calculating, modelling, theorizing, reproducing and institutionalizing inquiry. Scientific knowledge changes, but changes do not prove arbitrariness. In fact, the capacity for revision is the strength of science. The philosophical question is what is the criterion that separates science from non-science. The use of the only Many astronomical findings are made without direct controlled experiments. It is just that the mathematics Many areas of biology are observational, rather than mathematical. Karl Popper insisted on the rebuttal of scientific claims that possible evidence would disprove. However, the history of actual science shows that theories are not immediately discarded upon a single failed observation; instruments, supporting hypotheses, and data and methods are also examined. Thomas Kuhn discusses the crisis and paradigm-shifting of general science in the history of science. It would be wrong to call this idea that science is only fashion. Paradigms provide social and conceptual frameworks; however, the acceptance of new theories is not merely a power struggle; the effectiveness of problem-solving, prediction, interpretability, data, and research are crucial. When science deals with electrons, genes, quarks, curved spacetime or other indirect objects, the question arises whether all objects really are: are theories merely successful computational devices? Scientific realism says that successful theories often capture some aspect of the actual structure of the world. The instrumentalist view cautions that predicate-failure does not automatically prove absolute metaphysical truth. Parallel philosophy accepts not infallibility but evidence-based belief in the dispute. All we see are the facts: the sentence is simple. Scientific observation is connected to instruments, measurement methods, concepts, and background theory. However, this does not imply that the facts are arbitrary. Different teams can test one-two claims using the same tools, recursion, public statistics, and critical methods. Science looks for causal explanations, not just correlations. Causality is investigated by controlled experiments, natural experiments, statistical models, mechanistic explanations, and various methods. Hume 's advent-problem serves as a reminder that the conclusion from the past to the future is not philosophically sound. Modern science does not hide uncertainties; it organizes them by probability, confidence-interval, error, recursion, and independent verification. Science can tell which policies reduce pollution, which drugs are effective on average, and which technologies increase risk. But risk alone is justified; our interests are primary; we must make sacrifices; our ethical questions do not end with data alone. Facts inform value judgments. values do not cancel out facts. One extreme says that only science can answer all meaningful questions. Another says that epistemology is also an ideology, and therefore not a specific epistemological authority. Both of these are not right. The empirical method of science is extremely powerful in the questions of the natural world, disease, matter, biological processes, climate, and technological influence. But the question of justice, beauty, rights, the meaning of life and religious experience does not end with laboratory-assessment alone. Scientific theories do not simply summarize observed phenomena; they propose causes or structures, predict new outcomes, and sometimes enable interventions. These three functions are not the same. A model may give correct predictions but may misinterpret the reasons.A historical science may give strong explanations without precise control. The assessment of science will vary by subject. Planetary motion, disease distribution, geological history, and social behavior cannot be examined in the same laboratory. Multiplicity of law not evidentialism Transparent measurement and error-correction will be required in every field.

philosophyChapters.uttarapaksha: Changing can be a sign of improvement not failure. Reliability is built from the ability to perform tests, independent reviews, and revisions, rather than from infallibility.
philosophyChapters.synthesis: Parallel philosophy does not deify or discount science. Science is one of the best public methods of understanding the physical world. not the only source of moral value.

philosophyChapters.title: The Individual and Society
philosophyChapters.summary: A person is not born outside of society. Language and name, relationships, memory, education, business opportunities, fears, beliefs, and restrictions are all connected to the social world. But individuals are also not passive products of society. Individuals question, rebel, create new languages, reform traditions, and change institutions. The relationship between the individual and society is therefore not one-sided causality but a mutual construction. After birth, the child is not without social meaning as a ready-made independent self. One becomes a person by learning language, forming relationships, understanding rules, and accepting the social meaning of one 's body and identity. Our emotions are also affected by how we look. Family, caste, class, gender, language, region, and religion can define many occasions and boundaries. If all ideas are said to be merely social products, how is social criticism itself possible? Reformers, rebels, poets, scientists, philosophers, and ordinary citizens disagree with the norms of their societies. The social effect is real, not absolute. Parallel philosophy therefore accepts both individual autonomy and social status. Community gives people language, security, belonging, and meaning. But the community is not holy. Caste ostracism, misogynistic rules, violence over religious conversions, linguistic oppression, and destruction of autonomy in the name of family show that communities can be unjust themselves. The individual dignity should not be inferior to the community tradition. Liberal traditions emphasize the rights of the individual to elections and protection from the state. Community critics remind that the real person is not a disconnected atom. Their values, language, choices and identities are shaped by social history. Parallelism does not see this conflict as a choice of sides. Communities without rights can be tyrannical. person-stories without relationships can be imaginary. Human beings do not only want resources but also respect and recognition. Humiliation, untouchability, linguistic inferiority, caste stereotypes, and gender devaluation affect a person 's self-esteem. Social justice does not only mean income distribution. it also means the structure of respect. The digital medium has reshaped the way individuals socialize. Network communities, algorithmic visibility, group-learning, online humiliation, collective memory and disinformation change the individual-society relationship. The person may speak more, but may also be more subject to group pressure and information manipulation. To think of society as a sum of individuals, languages, currencies, laws, and traditions - facts that do not arise or cease at the whim of any one individual - is difficult. Conversely, if society were considered a free organism, individual suffering and responsibility would disappear. Proper analysis assumes emergent structures: those formed by the individual 's actions but giving actual effect to the individual 's choices after they are made. For example, markets are made up of millions of decisions; however, prices and employment conditions present themselves as external constraints to an individual. Family members are related, but inheritance and gender can be generational rules. To change the structure, one must change the collective rules with individual will. Be up to date on the evidence analysis. Statements by individuals can lead to institutional hypotheses, but broader claims must examine multiple experiences, norms, statistics, and historical changes. It is also a mistake to derive individual traits from group-level data. Human conduct does not merely learn from explicit commands; it lives within norms of ostentation, ridicule, and repetition. For this reason, unfair treatment can survive as a normal habit even if the law prohibits it. More than punishment, new examples, language and institutional incentives are necessary for social change. Imitation is not always a sign of oppression. Children learn language, cooperation and skills along the way. The question is whether standards are open to question or imposed as a birthright. Critical distance is the ability to see causes and consequences rather than dismissing one 's own traditions as external objects.

philosophyChapters.title: The Justification of the State
philosophyChapters.summary: The state orders, levies taxes, makes laws, imposes penalties, controls property, establishes borders, and sometimes uses force. For this reason, the fundamental philosophical question of the state is why this coercive power is justified. The state is there, so don 't take it as an excuse. Power and legitimacy are two different things. Hobbes fears a state of insecurity and seeks justification for strong sovereign power. Security is, of course, a basic requirement of political life. But security alone is not enough. Prisons can also be very safe, but not a free society. Security itself can become a source of fear for citizens if the state assumes unchecked power in the name of security. Locke justified political power in terms of the preservation of life, liberty, and property. The legitimacy of the government is linked to the consent and sovereignty of the governed. A serious contribution of this tradition is that the state is not the master of the citizen. the power of the government is purposeful and limited. Rousseau 's question is not merely one of fewer states: whose will does the law really express; if citizens themselves participate in law-making as equal members, the meaning of political obedience changes. But collectivism can become oppression when the majority or ruling class impose their will in the name of the common good. A law may be passed by due process, but may still be unfair. The history of slavery, caste exclusion, women 's rights-defying and colonial laws shows that legal legality and moral justice are not the same. Therefore, the duties of civil obedience are not absolutely unlimited. Parallel philosophy asks for a public reason from the state. Why is there a limit to freedom? Why should I do it? Why there is a need for surveillance Why the Land Acquisition Act Why the Language Policy? The reasons for decisions affecting the lives of citizens must be public, verifiable and fair on equal footing. The interests of the state are not the final answer. One view holds that the state should be limited primarily to protectionism, contracts, and rights-protection. Another view holds that real freedom requires education, health, social security, and a minimum of economic opportunities; therefore, the state must play a positive role. Parallel philosophy examines influence, resources, capability, and dignity in this debate. The more or less fundamental question is whether the state 's power is accountable, transparent and equally dignified. When power is highly centralized, local knowledge can override language and needs. But local power can also lead to caste, gender, or community oppression. Multicentric democracy, therefore, does not merely mean decentralisation. local autonomy + fundamental rights + responsibilities + judicial security. The state possesses extensive data collection expertise and coordination, but lacks the granular knowledge of local life. The Centre 's policies may fail to capture the imagination of the average person across diverse geographies and languages. The capacity of the state and ignorance must be acknowledged at the same time. A local consultation is not just a formal meeting after a decision has been made. Those affected may participate in defining the problem, making choices, and checking results. However, the local opinion itself is not factually accurate. there will be limits to independent measurement and authority. The epistemic polite state publishes reasons, formulates testable policies, admits errors and lays down ways for improvement. Continuing a failed policy to save face destroys public trust. Taxes are not just a forced reduction of a person 's wealth; they are the financing of social conditions - laws, money, roads, education and security. However, the powers of the state are not unlimited. The use and processing of the tax burden demands public justification. Equal pay sometimes creates a disproportionate burden because the same amount of living resources is reduced for individuals with lower incomes. Progressivity, consumption taxes, property taxes and service charges give different distributive results. Claims for justice should be checked against real data and administrative capacity.

philosophyChapters.title: Freedom
philosophyChapters.summary: Freedom does not mean the state alone cannot stop me. Individuals may be legally free, without real options due to hunger, debt, caste exclusion, patriarchy, illiteracy, violence, lack of disability-friendly structures, or societal fears. At the same time, freedom is destroyed again when the state or community takes over the choice of the individual in the name of real freedom. Freedom is therefore a concept with many layers. What 's holding me back from asking the fundamental question of negative freedom? Unnecessary repression, censorship, arbitrary arrests, religious compulsions, traffic restrictions, and the imposition of marriage-choice are all direct obstacles to freedom. Both the state and the community can be interventionist. Individuals must have a protected area where they can make decisions about their lives. Lack of inhibitions alone is not enough if a person does not have the minimum ability to achieve their goals. Education, health, food, information, physical safety and mobility all influence the real choice areas. Positive freedom emphasizes the question of what a person can actually do. But the danger is that the state may exercise patriarchal control, saying, " We know your real interests. " Capacity-building should, therefore, increase a person 's agency and not replace them. Freedom is not just the number of choices. A person 's ability to choose their values, relationships, professions, beliefs, language, religion or law, love, creation and life-plan is also important. Autonomy is not self-sufficiency without society. it is self-determination in the midst of information, ideas, relationships, and ample opportunities for self-examination. Extreme economic inequality can lead to a loss of legal freedom. On paper, both have the same market-independence, but neither has the same power to exchange when one person has no food options nor the vast resources of another. Conversely, strict controls to impose perfect equality may crush individuals ' choices. Parallel Philosophy Formula: Equality without liberty can become privilege. equality without liberty control. Our freedom is not allowed to destroy another person 's equal rights. Limitations may be appropriate in the context of hate, violence, harassment, fraud, public health or outright rights violations. However, the limit must be verifiable, proportional, and minimal. John Stuart Mill famously held that in civilised societies, personal restraint may be justified mainly to protect others from harm. The theory offers a powerful defense of diversity of expression, lifestyle, and personality. However, the definition of harm is not the same as severe emotional distress, economic impact, collective risk, disinformation, or structural injustice. Therefore, a detailed public argument is necessary. Informal rules of caste, gender, language, and religion are sometimes more stringent than the law itself. The law may allow inter-caste marriages but prevent family violence. the constitution may grant language rights but force social ridicule to give up the mother tongue. so freedom is not just a legal question. It is also necessary to change the social structure. Digital platforms increase expression, but surveillance and data-gathering create new problems of algorithmic control and information manipulation. Choice seems free, but if the structure of choice is dictated by invisible systems, then the question of autonomy arises again. Having many options does not automatically mean more freedom. The numbers give an illusion when all options are insecure, abusive or financially impossible. A reliable exit would sometimes be worth more than ten hypothetical options. The quality of the options is determined by information cost, risk, and return probability. The consumer will see many plans in the contract, but the choice is not free if the terms are ambiguous. Political elections have many names but limited freedom of information and fair competition. Ability-wise, this asks for a real chance to win. Measure the constraint while counting the policy options. The choice of the individual should be respected, but the consequences of a compelling circumstance should not be legitimized as a choice.

philosophyChapters.title: Equality
philosophyChapters.summary: Equality does not mean making all human beings uniform. It is fundamentally equality of moral status: every person possesses equal basic dignity, equal civic respect, and an equal claim to public justification. Modern political philosophy then raises a difficult question: equality of what—rights, opportunities, resources, capabilities, respect, or political influence? Without answering this question, “equality” can become a mere slogan. The talents, interests, body language, family circumstances, and life-plans of the two individuals may differ. Equality does not seek to eliminate these differences. The goal is for differences not to become the basis of dishonor, civility, or subjugation. Equal treatment is sometimes just, sometimes different help is needed because of unequal circumstances. Equality, therefore, is not the loss of one 's goods but the denial of a superior unqualified status without just cause. The law may say that all citizens are equal. This is a necessary achievement, but not sufficient. If access to education, health, land, capital, social interaction and safe public spaces is highly unequal, so too will the exercise of equal rights. For this reason, it is necessary to distinguish between formal equality and real equality of opportunity. Historical inequality does not end with simply saying that we are all equal. In a race, people are free to be tied down from generation to generation and then cut the rope until formal equality is a real justice. The Equal Opportunity ideal states that positions, education, and public opportunities should not be restricted by birthright. However, open competition alone is not enough if the initial conditions are too uneven. Nutrition becomes a precondition for school, language, social security, discrimination and family resource competition. So equality of opportunity demands an institutional precondition. Sharing resources equitably will not always lead to equal outcomes because individuals have different needs. The elderly, the disabled, children or socially disadvantaged individuals need extra support to live independently. The capability view emphasizes that the question should not only be about what one possesses but also what one can actually do and become. Parallel philosophy links this view to the dignity principle. Equality is not only a question of distribution; it is also a question of relation. If a group in a society is expected to touch another 's feet, use separate utensils, stay away from public places, or have a less valued voice in decisions, unequal civic relations can be avoided even with increased economic resources. Equality is therefore also a public rite of passage to those of us who share the same values. A person may work hard, but talent, family, health, birthplace, and historical occasion are not their choices. Accepting the role of effort in success, it is difficult to regard all results as having a purely moral merit. It is also unfair to call failure a character flaw. This argument does not exhaust the respect for achievement. The question is the extent of authority arising from the fruit. Outstanding work may be encouraged, as well as contributing to the original opportunity by acknowledging the debt they owe to society. Justice will decide which inequalities are useful and voluntary, and which are the dominions of arbitrary luck. The difference should be checked against actual data, the impact of incentives, and the minimum of dignity. Equal treatment of people with the same condition Horizontal equality. different help vertical equality according to different needs or abilities. Giving the same medicine to all patients can be both formal and medically inappropriate. Differential treatment can lead to discrimination, depending on the context. The category must be relevant to the actual purpose, to the extent necessary, and reviewable. The language of inborn prejudice should not be returned to as a different necessity. The transparency criterion is of particular importance. Both the beneficiary and the disadvantaged will understand why the distinction was made and how to appeal.

philosophyChapters.synthesis: Equality, not uniformity, is the principle of ensuring equal moral status, equal civic dignity, and fair opportunities and real capabilities. The formula for the parallel philosophy: birth is not a moral qualification.

philosophyChapters.title: Justice
philosophyChapters.summary: It is not just about dispensing justice. Honor is also justice. There is also the matter of representation. They will also be able to listen in. There is also the issue of due process. Also a correction of the injustices of history. Justice asks who gets what, why, how to make decisions, how to make rules and bear the burden of rules. A person can act justly or unjustly. also laws and institutions. In modern societies, education, health, property, police, courts, elections, labour market and family norms shape life opportunities. For this reason, justice is not only a personal virtue but also a criterion of social structure. Distributive justice asks for fair sharing of resources, opportunities, burdens and benefits. Equal sharing, need-based sharing, merit and contribution, and free exchange all present different theories. No single theory is sufficient in every field. According to emergency medicine requirements and award achievements, civil rights can equally demand different things. Rawls 's hypothesized origins provide a means to think objectively, removing information about the person 's social identity, wealth, race, gender, and talents. Its strength is that a person chooses rules when he does not know where he will be born in society. Parallel philosophy finds this fiction useful, but at the same time asks how much of the real injustices of history can be understood only through imaginary fairness. Who sits at the table to decide what is right? If the principle of justice is built without the voice of the victim, then the fairness of the principle must be re-examined. Representation is more than just numbers; it requires effective participation, language access, information, and real influence on decisions. Correct results are not enough if the process is opaque, biased or abusive. Hearing, reasoned judgment, appeals, common law, and conflict-of-interest disclosures are all part of procedural justice. Public hearings are an important form of civic respect from the courthouse to the school. The injustices of the past can survive by becoming the structures of the present. The effects of history can be passed down through generations, from land-grabbing to slavery to caste-abuse to education and women 's property. Corrective justice is seeking institutional answers by identifying the historical sources of existing inequality, not retribution. People often say that a worthy person will receive his fruits. But what is merit based on: effort, contribution, necessity, sacrifice, or discipline? This criterion gives a different result. It is hard to complete the same distributions all at once. Measuring effort is difficult because opportunities and abilities are different. Contributions do not equate to market value; care workers are paid less than is necessary for society. The emphasis on necessity begs the question of incentive. Justice is not a blind application of a principle. Criteria should be clear by region: achievement in awards, need in health care, and equal status in civil rights. The reason why the category changes is also different. Punishment of crimes may aim for retribution, deterrence, reform, social security or victim recognition. A tool does not serve all purposes in the same way. While harsher penalties are popular, they can be ineffective in reducing crime. The appropriate penalty should be proportional to the fault and the harm caused, in terms of intent and procedure. Reducing the risk to the innocent is the paramount prerequisite because wrongful convictions cannot be reversed. Poor legal aid to the poor can make similar laws unequal. A guilty person does not lose his or her dignity. Rehabilitation, education and the possibility of returning to society can be a means of preventing future harm, not of undermining justice. Restorative perspectives view crime not only as a violation of the law but as a loss to the individual and the relationship. The needs of the victim, the responsibility of the offender and community improvement are brought into the dialogue. It is not appropriate for every crime. Reconciliation pressure on victims of power imbalances or violence can cause other harm. Participation must be voluntary, security strong and legal rights protected.

philosophyChapters.title: Caste and Social Hierarchy
philosophyChapters.summary: Caste is not just a personal prejudice but a historical social construct. Caste long determined opportunities in marriage, labour, education, status, residence, religious rights, and social interaction. The question of caste-philosophy, therefore, is not merely a question of whether or not people like each other but of the relationship between birth and moral status. The answer to the parallel philosophy is clear: birth is not a moral qualification. If a tradition denies the equal dignity of human beings, then criticism of the tradition is morally justified. The antiquity of the tradition proves its historical importance, not moral expediency. Division of labour is sometimes argued in favour of caste. But the question arises as to why the act of circumcision should be congenital. Why the freedom to change profession is limited Why is there a hierarchy of marriage, food, education, residence and respect? For this reason, the problem of caste is not merely an economic one but one of social conditioning and hereditary status. Untouchability creates social distance by declaring the human body unclean. It is not just religious considerations that can determine actual access to water, roads, schools, temples, homes, food, marriage and labour. At this level, dignity is not an abstract term; it is the public presence of the body. Ambedkar does not criticise caste solely through appeals to harmony; he raises questions of social structure, religious appropriateness, intermarriage and political representation. Castration is not merely the reduction of an offending behavior but the breaking of a closed, birth-based structure. Laws are necessary to prohibit discrimination, grant rights, and ensure representation. But social habits, marriage-network, economic dependence, linguistic insults and cultural prestige alone do not change laws instantly. Parallel philosophy, therefore, sees a combined program of legal equality, social reform, education, representation, and economic opportunity. Sanitation, ritual purification and social untouchability are different concepts. Hygiene of disease-prevention asking for empirical reasons. ritual purification meaning of community. inborn impurities of man. direct opposition to equal dignity. Calling all three the same avoids discrimination in the language of health or religion. A profession may be associated with dirty conditions, but workers are not dirty people. Secure equipment requires a decent wage and division of labor. It is a double injustice to have a birthright. An internal reinterpretation of the tradition is useful but does not oblige the victim to wait for correction. The law required that public service and social education run concurrently. Housing segregation affects access to schools, roads, markets and social networks. Social boundaries can be strict, with distances on maps being short. The location forms the physical form of the hierarchy. Segregation does not have to end just because income increases. Land tenure, rent discrimination, public investment and fear of violence must be checked. The structure can vary between villages and towns. The spatial study map should include demographics and service data. Ensure equal access to public facilities while maintaining the privacy of your private home. Subtle insults may seem trivial at first glance, but constant repetition has a cumulative effect on education, health, and self-confidence. Evidence is not just a single event. it is a sample of behavior and the organization 's response and results. The assumption that every unpleasant behavior is due to caste also calls for caution. Comparative situations and unequal application of spoken word rules and other evidence should be examined. The victim 's statement is the primary evidence at the outset, not the sole evidence at the end. Complaint-Method Provides secure recording of evidence before it is destroyed, preventing retaliation and explaining the reasons for the decision. Silence is not evidence of an absence of complaint if the complaint is costly. Urbanization, education, and markets can loosen old occupational limits; therefore, time will provide solutions that do not require major reform.

philosophyChapters.title: Class and Economic Power
philosophyChapters.summary: Property does not just create private convenience; it also creates power. Those who control resources, land, capital, information or technology, have an influence on social decisions. The question of economic philosophy is not merely one of the quantity of money but of control and dependence, of bargaining power and democratic equality. In the Marxist tradition, class is understood by its relation to the means of production. The relation of master and worker is not merely one of income-interference; it is a question of decision, risk, control of labour, and ownership of surplus. In the modern economy, managers, professionals, unorganised workers, platform-based labour and financial capital make this structure more complex. Labour is not merely commodity-production but man 's time and life. The ethical implications of voluntary contractual agreements can be undermined if the worker 's working conditions are set in unsafe, abusive or completely unequal bargaining positions. Economic freedom has to be judged by real choices. Extreme economic power can amplify political voices through media, election finance, lobbying, expertise, data, and legal resources. The formal equality of one person and one vote is undermined if money becomes an almost direct means of political influence. Poverty can lead to a lack of food, health, housing, education, mobility, time, security, and social respect. Competence-vision therefore looks at actual life expectancy rather than income. Class analysis is necessary, but not sufficient. Race, gender, language, region, and religion influence the distribution of economic opportunity. Two people of the same income may have different real status because of Social Security, inheritance, networks, or discrimination. Market-wage implies demand-supply and not moral sufficiency. Contracts are formal, voluntary and not dignified if full-time employment but also food, housing, health, and education is impossible. The measure of the living wage varies by family size, regional cost and public service. One number does not apply to all places. Empirical studies are needed to see if the increase affects employment. Along with salary, time, security, leave, and respect also make up the quality of work. A high income does not automatically justify a dangerous or abusive situation. A worker may be vulnerable to a large employer; the organization balances out the strengths. The right to form associations, to share information and to enter into collective agreements enhances the genuine spontaneity of the contract. The Union itself is not immune from liability. Internal democracy, financial transparency, the right to dissent and the interests of unorganised workers are essential. Leadership did not have to be a permanent privilege. Strikes impose costs on employers and the public, and their justification must be judged by the goal and process, the safety of essential services, and the options available. Mass pressure is not violence, but it is also not without limits. Debt provides future income for current needs, but unclear interest rates, mortgages, and emergency forces can create long-term dependency. The borrower 's willingness to compromise is often undermined by a lack of information and options. Not all interest is absorbed; the time and risk and administrative costs are real. The question is the ratio of the rate, the transparency, the method of recovery and the power of the lender. Financial literacy is useful, but not a substitute for structural regulation. The contract must be legible, comparable, and free from abusive charges. It is argued that criticism of economic inequality breeds envy of successful individuals and reduces motivation to produce. It is truly inadequate to consider injustice merely in terms of difference. The answer is that class-criticism examines not only the wealth of the individual but also the conditions of labor, opportunity, property, and political influence. The question is who holds more, and whether their excesses constitute subordination to others. Create appropriate criticism by acknowledging the contribution of risk and effort, as well as hereditary privilege and monopoly, and accounting for external costs.

philosophyChapters.title: Women, Gender, and Power
philosophyChapters.summary: In philosophical history, the word man became synonymous with the experience of men in practice several times. Control over a woman 's body, labour, reproduction, property, education and public appearance must be considered philosophical questions. Feminist philosophy does not have a uniform creed; liberal, socialist, radical, postcolonial, Dalit, intersectional and many other strands raise different questions. Traditional political philosophies focused on the state and the market, leaving the family as the personal domain. But in the family, there is property, care, violence, marriage, reproduction, education, and the distribution of opportunities. So power within the home is not outside political philosophy. How free is a person to make decisions about their body? Marriage, pregnancy, health, clothing, mobility and sexual consent are all areas of struggle for autonomy and social norms. Autonomy is not just about declaring options; it is also about the absence of coercion, dependence, violence and social punishment. Home care, childcare, eldercare, food, and sanitation are the foundation of the rural labor economy but are often invisible in economic statistics. If a group 's time is systematically spent in unpaid care, their education, employment, leisure and political participation are affected. Despite legal equality, barriers to employment, education, succession, leadership, and public safety remain. Having the same rules is not enough if the institution is based on a historically male way of life. Women are not a homogeneous social class. Caste, class, religion, language, region, disability and other identities alter gender experiences. Therefore, it is not appropriate to declare a single feminine experience as universal. The multidisciplinary method of parallel philosophy is particularly useful here because the experiences are different but share a common criterion of dignity. Theories about the absence of women may leave some experiences unexplained. For this reason, representation is not just a question of political seats; it is also a question of knowledge. What experiences are considered to be the experiences of ordinary human beings is the subject of philosophical introspection. Traditional politics may regard the home as private and the state-market as public. But within the home, labour-distribution, education, property and violence make up public capacity. Privacy can protect inequality by keeping it out of the law. This criticism does not justify the state 's unlimited access. Intimacy is valued in the realm of love and personal decision-making. Interference should be minimal based on obvious harm, dependence and entitlement. Secrecy can be a protection for the victim, not a shield for the criminal. Confidential channels of complaint and impartial investigation balance this dichotomy. Decisions about the body are central to an individual 's autonomy; consent is essential in medicine, reproduction, marriage, and sex. The interests of the family, the community or the state cannot merely make the body of the individual a means. Autonomy Information and services can exist without paperwork. Secure healthcare, privacy, and financial access make for better decision-making. Where another life or public health is affected, the dispute is complex. The proof should explain the harm ratio and the minimum deterrent measures. Moral disagreement should not turn into humiliation. Language can gender the image of occupational rights and normal human beings. Positions that are exclusively male influence the prospects for children and social expectations. But grammatical gender and social discrimination are not the same thing. The changes must take into account linguistic structure, living use, and speaker convenience. Forced castration may prevent arousal of public opinion. Inclusive language is a complement to structural reform. The positions are subject to change as well as opportunities for recruitment, security, and leadership. After the laws are declared equal, the remaining difference is said to be the result of a private election. Formal rights are a historic achievement, but the cost of use, fear of violence, the burden of care and the professional trap can still change choices.

philosophyChapters.title: Language, Region, and Identity
philosophyChapters.summary: The language is more of a medium of communication. The language has a unique way of looking at history, memory, humor, love, folklore, religious experiences, labor terminology, family relationships, and the world. For this reason, the question of language is not only a question of grammar; it is also a question of dignity and access, of representation and structure. Individuals share many identities: linguistic, regional, religious, occupational, ethnic, sexual, and national. Linguistic identity is an important dimension of all of these, but no single identity is synonymous with the whole person. Parallelism cautions against the politics of single-labelism. Languages give identity, but they do not have to be fences. The language of childhood forms the initial world of thought. If the instruction is in a completely unfamiliar language, the language barrier is added to the content. However, mother tongue-based education and comprehensive multilingualism are not antagonistic goals. Appropriate policies strengthen the intellectual base in the local language while increasing access to other useful languages. The question is not one of language or another language. the question is just multilingualism. Access to knowledge is determined by what language the state, universities, courts, markets, technology and publications prefer. If the language of the citizen is constantly absent from public institutions, their experience may become invisible. Linguistic justice is not just a symbolic honour; it is also an opportunity for translation, education, administrative access, digital support and publication. Regional identity preserves local history, ecology, language and memory. But if regional pride becomes the demeanour of another region, that is not self-respect but a new form of dominance. The principle of parallel philosophy is clear: respect for one 's own identity must be compatible with equal dignity with that of others. Mithila 's language-literature, scriptures, folk traditions, and cross-border cultural life show that political boundaries and cultural geography are not always synonymous. The study of such a regional world makes broader history more nuanced than nationalism. But every claim to historical glory must pass the test of proof. Digital tools like small language publishing, audio-visual collections, dictionaries and e-magazines provide new opportunities for learning and archiving. At the same time, artificial intelligence and standardized data give more advantages to languages with multiple sources. Therefore, Unicode 's free font and corpus require quality translations and local content for digital linguistic justice. Living languages change with borrowing, new words, and migration. By treating change as a fall every time, language becomes a museum object. Unchecked dominance, on the other hand, can reduce local vocabulary. Authenticity is not finding a pure origin. it is meaningful continuity through community. The need of the hour is to check comprehension and consistency with Maithili grammar. Make sure that there are options available. Dictionaries both describe and guide, but do not govern, living experiments. The standard is developed through literature, school and mass media communication. Some languages form the basis of employment, examinations and prestige. Intergenerational transmission of mother tongues may be impaired as families choose the dominant language for useful occasions. It is the result of structural incentives, not just emotional apathy. They should not be made opponents of employment to save the mother tongue. Bilingual education, publication, digital means and use in public services give practical value to the language. If linguistic pride stops learning a second language, the child 's opportunities will decrease. The goal is multilingualism and not isolationist purity. Scripts are associated with both cultural memory and access to texts. Preservation of historical scripts is important, but so too is access to education and digital literacy. Respecting one option does not necessarily mean destroying the other. Cataloguing old manuscripts requires high-quality copies and reading-training. A symbolic celebration alone would not have preserved the record.

philosophyChapters.title: Democracy
philosophyChapters.summary: Democracy is not just about elections. If elections are held but critics remain fearful, if parliament is there but institutions are ineffective, if majority is there then minority rights are insecure, if constitution is there but social relations survive on humiliation then democracy is incomplete. The first meaning of democracy is that state power derives legitimacy from the citizens. But democracy itself is not uniform. The Constitution 's Fundamental Rights limit the power of the majority. Both majority rule and rights-protection are necessary. Representation is not just about counting the votes. The question is which community is present at the site of the decision. What experiences are consistently missed The number and form of representation may vary by geographical area, gender, marginalized communities, and linguistic groups. The quality of democracy should also be measured by how much power listens to social diversity. An independent judiciary, legislature, independent journalism, electoral process, universities, civil society and information are the structural foundations of democracy. Leaders are popular and not above the company. Personal goodwill is not a substitute for institutional control. One hard virtue of democracy is to regard the opposition not as the enemy, but as the legitimate opposition. Public argument ends when disagreement is interpreted as treason or immorality or moral turpitude. Parallel philosophies regard democracy as a public order with constant scriptural pressure and counter-pressure, evidence, criticism, and revision. Political equal suffrage is extremely important, but civil equality is incomplete when the society suffers from birth defects, economic subjugation, or gender-based violence. For this reason, social democracy is the basis of political democracy. Misinformation, propaganda, artificial materials, and algorithmic polarization influence democratic decisions. Solutions require not just censorship but also source-checking, media-literacy, transparency, independent fact-checking, and civic conscience. Elections renew the regime 's authorization from time to time, but decisions are made continuously in the intervening period. Responsibility is weakened when the citizen 's role is limited to one vote in five years. Hearing, right to information, local assemblies, committees and peaceful protests are the means of sustained democracy. Not all subjects are referendum-eligible; complex decisions require expertise and delegate time. Too much involvement can lead to burnout and the domination of organized oligarchies. The process should be relevant, accessible, and representative. The opposition is not the enemy of the regime; it presents an alternative and makes regime change possible. A democracy without a permanent opposition can dominate while having elections. The duty of the opposition is not just to obstruct. Factual criticism considers possible alternatives and constitutional limitations. Extremism that destroys every institution in the name of silence and protest in the name of national interest. Finance decisions and internal democracy of both the ruling and opposition parties should be open to public scrutiny. Free speech is when citizens have access to reliable information and a variety of options. Systematic falsehoods distort the will to choose the fake medium or source-cover election. The risk of censorship if the state becomes the sole arbiter of truth. Independent fact-checking, media-transparency, source-marking, and prompt response may be better tools. The law must be limited, without cause, and appealable if it is manifestly violent. Medium-literacy is a long-term solution, but so is the creative responsibility of the platform. The user should not be blamed entirely. Complex policies demand scientific and economic knowledge; ordinary voters do not know the details. Therefore, it seems attractive to offer a decision to an expert. Experts may offer superior knowledge on means-effects but aim for risk-distribution and fairness values. Experts are also intrigued by institutions and uncertainties. The civic experience gives the necessary knowledge of the implementation.

philosophyChapters.title: Gandhi
philosophyChapters.summary: In Gandhi 's philosophy, the relationship between truth, non-violence, satyagraha, and Swaraj, self-restraint and resourcefulness is central. They must be studied critically, not in the simplistic binary of worship or refutation. Gandhi Heritage Portal preserves original texts like * Hind Swaraj: * Satyagraha in South Africa: * Constructive Programme: * It is more appropriate to read Gandhi-Thought on the basis of these texts. For Gandhi, truth is not only factual correctness but also moral practice. A person is not an absolute master of truth. he is a seeker of truth. This makes the language of introspection and experimentation important in his writing. Parallel philosophy takes from this a lesson in epistemic humility, but retains the usual criterion of proof in questions of public fact. Ahimsa is not the absence of inaction. Silence in the face of injustice is not the ideal of nonviolence; the aim is to challenge injustice without resorting to violence. But the moral high ground of nonviolence raises difficult questions when immediate life-saving or state repression or community violence is present. It is therefore necessary to discuss both the historical consequences and the moral limits of nonviolence. Satyagraha is the political method of addressing one 's conscience rather than destroying the opposition. Self-sacrifice, discipline, public speaking, and the morality of means are the foundations of this method. In contrast to violent conquests, satyagraha viewed opponents as fellow citizens of the future. In Hind Swaraj, Swaraj is not merely the end of foreign rule; it is also a question of self-rule, civilisational review and the discipline of the will. Gandhi takes a critical look at the pace of modern industrial civilization, at consumption and centralization, and at machine-driven life. But some of his findings on modern medicine, technology, industrialisation and village-wise demand rigorous revision today. Gandhi 's crucial plea is that unjust means corrupt the just ends. This principle is particularly important in political ethics: lying in the name of truth, terror in the name of freedom, and insult in the name of equality do not automatically sanctify the injustice of the language of the instrument. Gandhi 's views on caste changed over time, but Ambedkar 's critique of it would be incomplete without a study. Opposing untouchability is not enough if the inherent caste-structure itself is out of the question. Parallel philosophies read Gandhi and Ambedkar not as conflicting icons but as rigorous philosophical dialogues. The satyagrahi possesses the moral strength to awaken the conscience of the opponent by taking risks with his body. But self-pity can sometimes become emotional pressure, especially when followers take risks with leadership commands. Volunteering and information is a must. Leaders cannot make the sacrifice of others their moral capital. The distribution of risk should be a clear condition of protection for vulnerable participants and prevention of exposure. Self-compassion is bravery, not a devaluation of life. The conclusion that greater suffering is more likely to be true if the outcome is not achieved is unfair. The re-evaluation of means should be part of the introspection of satyagraha. Resistance weakens unjust institutions, but without alternatives, old power can fill the void. Education, sanitation, local production, community cooperation and constructive work against untouchability make up the potential of future societies. Local self-sufficiency is not complete economic isolation. What can be locally justified and what can be widely supported must be decided by evidence. Romantic village-dramas do not hide the drudgery and caste inequality. The success of constructive programs must be measured by participation, resource sustainability, and the real rights of vulnerable groups; symbolic labor is not enough. The person may sometimes refuse to obey the law for serious moral reasons. Respect for conscience is essential, but not every private belief can be exempt from public law. Check the rights of others and the functionality of the shared entity.

philosophyChapters.title: Ambedkar
philosophyChapters.summary: At the heart of Ambedkar 's philosophy are social democracy, caste-free constitutionalism, representation, liberty, equality and fraternity. His writing considers social stigmatization as an institutional problem rather than just a moral evil. In Annihilation of Caste, Ambedkar does not criticise caste solely on the basis of economic backwardness. Caste is the structure of birth rank, intermarriage, social distance, and status. For this reason, formal equality of opportunity is not sufficient unless social institutions determine a person 's life path based on birth. Ambedkar 's important argument is that political freedom cannot replace social equality. Social democracy is necessary for political democracy to survive. For Indian public life, this question is as fundamental as the question of whether democracy is incomplete if social dignity is unequal. Ambedkar considers these three theories to be a trilogy, not separate entities but interdependent. Liberty without equality may become the privilege of the powerful; liberty without equality is difficult to maintain in social life. His public statements and writings consider this trilogy to be the foundation of democratic life. citeturn707669search25turn707669search28 A constitution is not just a legal document. it is a framework for rule over power, protection of rights and civil equality. Ambedkar stresses the importance of the constitutional method while warning that political democracy cannot survive in the serious paradox of socio-economic inequality. The representation of groups that have historically been excluded from decision-making is not just a question of symbolic presence. Representation is also a question of knowledge, which leads to experience in policy-making. Parallel philosophy takes up from here the question of who sits at the judging table. Ambedkar studies religion in relation to social morality, not just personal beliefs. Acceptance of Buddhism late in life was associated with questions of social dignity, moral community, and freedom. Treating the issue as merely a political strategy is insufficient. Both are against injustice but have serious differences of opinion on the social structure and methods of change. Gandhi emphasizes self-transformation, moral appeal, and community-reform.Ambedkar on legal rights, representation, structural change, and a clear program of annihilation of caste. Parallel philosophy studies both, questions both, and considers the dignity of the victim as the ultimate moral criterion. Some reforms may reduce the harshness of discrimination, but the basic structure survives if caste group-border intermarriage and status persist. Abolition is not merely a change of heart; it is a question of social reconstruction. Law, education, economic opportunity and inter-group relations must go together. Symbolic courtship is useful, but the effect is limited unless property, representation, and the actual barriers to marriage are changed. The leadership of change must come from the oppressed community; willing external allies will not reassert their dominance. Ambedkar 's conversion to Buddhism should be read as a project of social equality and new communities with individual spiritual choice. Their interpretation is not merely a revision of ancient Buddhist doctrine but a modern ethico-political re-reading. According to the historical Buddha, the later traditions and modern Navayana versions are different sources. Do not accuse one of the other. The validity of the recension must be checked with its stated modern purpose. Religion here claims to be a public discipline of dignity and fraternity rather than a means of accepting one 's destiny. Whether the claims constitute equality in practice is open to review. Liberation movements may ask for effective leadership, but by putting the leader above criticism, the institution is weakened. The merit of the opinion lies in examining the arguments by reading their texts and not in making citations the final order. Hero worship absolves the follower of responsibility and breeds succession conflicts. Organization rules should protect elections, collective leadership, and dissent.

philosophyChapters.uttarapaksha: True. the law is not enough. But without laws, representation, and institutional rights, social moral change can be weak. Both law and social order are necessary for justice to prevail.
philosophyChapters.synthesis: Ambedkar 's philosophy takes democracy beyond the ballot box to social relations, dignity, representation and fraternity. The Indian modern philosophical basis for this formulation of the philosophy of ijnana not being a moral qualification derives its depth from Ambedkar 's conception of caste.

philosophyChapters.title: What Is Religion?
philosophyChapters.summary: It is difficult to bind religion within a single definition. Belief? Ritual? Ethics? Community? A path to liberation? Sacred experience? A way of life? Each tradition combines these elements in different proportions. The first task of philosophy of religion, therefore, is to acknowledge the plurality of the word “dharma.” The history of the term Western modern religion and the semantics of Indian religions are not entirely identical. Dharma can mean duty, moral order, way of life, virtues, religious traditions, or social norms. Buddhism, Jainism, Vedic religion, the bhakti-tradition, and modern institutional religion do not share the same structure. The translation is the philosophical decision here. In some religions, theism is central, but it is inconsistent to define Buddhist or Jain traditions by the criterion of theism. So religion = God - belief is not a sufficient definition. Religion is expressed through group rituals, festivals, meals, mourning, marriages, pilgrimages, music, and stories and institutions. Here, religion is not just a theory but a social practice. But because social practice is ancient, it is not automatically moral. Every practice can be tested on the test of dignity and justice. Religious experiences can be profound, transformative, and meaningful for individuals. Philosophy may respect empirical truths, but does not automatically draw universal metaphysical conclusions from experience. If the experiences of different traditions claim different things, then additional arguments are necessary. Religion can give moral motivation, compassion, service, truth, and restraint. But religion says it is not the only answer to public moral righteousness, especially in a plural society. If religious rules deny someone equal dignity, then there is a right to criticism. Religious identity can be a source of language, memory, and connection for individuals and communities. But a person can be a dissenter, reformist, convert, or irreligious within their own tradition. Therefore, the right to a religious community should not extinguish an individual 's freedom of conscience. The Parallel Philosophy proposes three levels of separation in theology: personal faith. community religious life. state public law. Individual faiths should enjoy wide freedom, and community life should be subject to equal rights; the state should not make any one religious truth a condition of citizenship. Placing religion, magic, and science at the bottom of a simple hierarchy reduces the diversity of history. In the same society, ritual means technical knowledge and causal beliefs can coexist. Empirical claims call for scientific tests to see if the drug reduces the disease. The grief-meaning or communal memory of life is not a laboratory question. Segregation is not an insult; it is the selection of evidence. Criticism is necessary when there is harm, fraud or delay in treatment due to magical reasons. Religious freedom is not an unqualified right to another 's life. Myths tell the story of the community 's origins, values, and worldview. They cannot mean a chronology of history. Symbolic truths can open up human experience, although literal phenomena are not verifiable. To call a myth a complete lie is not to consider it a literary-religious work; to call it a history is a proof-class fallacy. The reader should clarify whether they are interpreting the cultural meaning of the story or an anecdotal one. The power of myth can also be a valid one. The moral of the story is to question whose origins are glorious and whose service is natural. Temples, monasteries, and shrines distribute donations and festive resources, labor, and prestige. Religious institutions can be not only groups of thinkers but also economic agents. Charity may be voluntary compassion, but social pressure or opaque use may constitute exploitation. The accounts must be maintained in accordance with the Public Standards Body for Asset Management and Service Delivery. Economic analysis does not reduce beliefs to profit calculations. They only show that sacred purpose is connected with practical resourcefulness.

philosophyChapters.title: The Question of God
philosophyChapters.summary: The question of God is one of the oldest and most enduring questions in philosophy. But whether there is a God is not the only question. It is first necessary to explain what is meant by God. The Creator The omniscient and omnipotent moral being The Reason for the World The Absolute Reality of the Absolute Nullity of Brahman A personal tribute to the or the symbolic center of religious experience. Different traditions take the word God to have different meanings; therefore, logic also varies in meaning. The concept of God is not uniform in Indian philosophy. The later acharyas of the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition, particularly Udayana, develop speculative arguments in favour of the existence of God. The classical form of Samkhya explains the world through the elements of Prakriti and Purusha and does not consider the creator God as indispensable. Purva-mimamsa tries to protect the authenticity of the Vedas without the need for a God-writer. Major schools of Buddhist philosophy do not accept a need for a creator God. Even within Vedanta, there are serious differences of opinion on the relationship between Brahman, Ishvara, and the world and the living entity. The first lesson to be drawn from this variety is that Indian philosophy is theistic or that Indian philosophy is atheistic; this is an oversimplification. The correct approach is to ask tradition-specific questions. A common argument in favor of God is based on causality: the world is changing, connected, or dependent; therefore, there must be a sufficient reason for it. Various forms of inference from intelligent agents developed within the juridical tradition, considering the world as work. In Western philosophy, there are several forms of cosmological reasoning: first cause, necessary being, sufficient cause, etc. But the objection immediately arises: if everything needs a cause, then what is the cause of God? In response, theists often say that reason is not the cause of all things but the cause of everything that exists or is possible. This answer does not eliminate the problem. The question remains, why can 't the universe itself be necessary? The reason why the chain is not infinite Whether it is right to apply the principle of causality to the whole universe Parallel philosophy does not consider this argument to be deductive or immediately deductive. Each line of reasoning must be tested separately. Intelligent planners have been inferred from the order of the world, mathematical structures, biological complexity, or life-adapting conditions. The power of this argument lies in its questioning of the comprehensibility and structure of the world. But natural selection, self-organization, physical laws, and the vast cosmic scale provide natural explanations for many complex phenomena. The philosophical question is therefore not as simple as the question of īlātilāt = God. The question is whether the existence or intelligibility of a final law demands additional interpretation when a natural explanation is available. The theists and naturalists differ on this point. Some thinkers associate material moral values or duties with the existence of God. If indeed some actions are not merely a question of choice but objectively improper, what is the ultimate basis for them? The theists may answer that the divine nature is full of auspiciousness. Objection: If an action is right only because God commands it, then morality can be arbitrary. if God commands what is right because it is freely right, then the basis of morality seems separate from God. This ancient dichotomy is a serious problem for religious morality. Parallel philosophy here regards the equal dignity of human beings as a public moral criterion. Religious morality may inspire, but the justification of a citizen 's rights cannot depend on sect-specific injunctions alone. A person experiencing prayer, meditation, devotion, mystical oneness, and purity considers this experience as evidence of God. It is unfair to call experience a direct illusion because experience is a real human event. However, the interpretation of the experience is disputed. Practitioners of different religions report different ultimate selves or realizations of truth. Psychological, social, and neurological explanations are also possible.

philosophyChapters.purvapaksha: The Question of God Eliminated from Science According to this view, the scientific explanation of natural phenomena, by extension, eliminates the need for God.
philosophyChapters.uttarapaksha: The level of the question is different. With the progress of logic and science, the gods of certain realms become weaker. But the philosophical question of God touches not only on what physical processes produce phenomena but also on questions of existence, causality, value, consciousness, and ultimate interpretation. Just because something is a philosophical question does not make God perfect. Science and metaphysics communicate on a different level. The State of Parallel Philosophy The question of God can neither be settled by ridicule nor by fear. The philosopher 's respect for the positions of the theist, atheist, and agnostic is when he explains his reasons, listens to the opposition, and accepts uncertainty honestly.
philosophyChapters.synthesis: God-criticism is not a yes / no vote but a multi-layered philosophical field of reason, morality, experience, suffering, freedom and interpretation. Parallelism does not privilege theism, nor does it automatically regard atheism as an intellectual triumph. Equal access to evidence, strong opposition, and dignified dialogue are the basic tenets of this chapter.
